_comment: Recording of live run 55 (status done); the plan is the model's own words.

steps.message: Reviewing the intake and the question.

claims.text: Goal: cut electricity bought from the grid by 30% by 2030 at P.S. 38, 421 Lincoln Avenue, Staten Island, on a $600,000 capital budget set for 2027.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Efficiency only does not reach the goal: it is estimated to cut grid use by 6.2% to 17.6%, which is 21% to 59% of the 30% goal.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Efficiency plus a budget-sized solar array reaches the goal in the model: an estimated 53.6% to 69.7% cut in grid use, and the typical cost range tops out at exactly the $600,000 budget, so there is no room for extras such as roof work.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The full path (deeper efficiency, the whole roof array and a backup battery) is estimated to cover 100% of annual use, but costs $276,486 to $826,967 more than the budget. Whether to extend the budget is the owner's decision once the gap is compared with the savings.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: These are planning estimates with wide ranges, not quotes or promises of savings. Payback figures are simple payback, not a full solar financial model.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: As entered: P.S. 38 (R038), an elementary school built in 1955, 17,620 sq ft of floor area, a flat roof of 34,360 sq ft, served by Con Edison. Annual grid electricity is 284,403 kWh (kWh is energy over time).
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: No existing solar, other renewables or efficiency work were entered, so the plan assumes none are in place. Please say so if any exist, because existing work would lower the savings available.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The baseline for the goal is the electricity the building buys from the grid. With no existing solar, it equals total electricity use.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: The city's tax-lot record (tax lot number, BBL, 5037320006) shows 17,620 sq ft of gross floor area, one floor, a 65,000 sq ft lot, no landmark flag, and three buildings on the lot.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: City building outlines on the lot total 34,363 sq ft across three buildings (19,757, 13,319 and 1,287 sq ft). This is ground area under the buildings, not a measured roof, and it is close to the 34,360 sq ft roof area entered.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's 2024 energy report (Local Law 84) for this lot lists electricity of 284,403 kWh, the same as the figure entered, an energy use per square foot (EUI) of 53.0 kBtu (thousand BTU), and an ENERGY STAR score of 74. It also lists natural gas of 512,500 kBtu and fuel oil of 1,476,599.8 kBtu.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's energy report covers 55,860 sq ft of floor area for two school records (R038 and R816), while the intake and tax-lot record show 17,620 sq ft. The 284,403 kWh may therefore cover more than the 17,620 sq ft building. Please confirm which buildings the bills cover.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's school solar-readiness assessment (Local Law 24) lists the owner as the Department of Education, status Not Solar Ready, roof condition Fair, and roof age 20 years or more.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Solar output range: system losses of 18% (low) to 10% (high) around the standard 14% default; weather is typical-year data.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Usable roof is taken as 55% of the roof area, to leave room for edges, equipment and access.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: The array needs about 66 sq ft of usable roof per kW of panels (kW is how much power at one moment).
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Battery size is an estimate: the critical load was not given, so it is taken as 1.0 watt per sq ft x 17,620 sq ft = 17.6 kW (not metered); backup length was not given, so 8 hours is assumed; battery energy is kW x hours / 0.85 round-trip efficiency = 166 kWh.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Efficiency measures (LED lighting and controls) are assumed to save 10-20% of annual use. This is a planning estimate, not a cited benchmark and not a building model.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Prices are planning-level benchmarks, not quotes: solar $2,528-3,752 per kW from the middle half of 239 completed NYC non-residential projects of 100-500 kW since 2022 (NYSERDA data); battery $546-812 per kWh from the middle half of 56 NYC storage projects; efficiency $1.17-4.02 per kWh saved a year (standard) and $1.09-3.83 (deep) from completed NYC public-sector projects. The efficiency savings percents (10-20% standard, 15-25% deep) are planning estimates, and only 62%-88% of them is counted because the City's audited projects delivered that share (Local Law 87 report, DCAS, FY2022).
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Baseline: 284,403 kWh a year of grid electricity, entered by the user and matching the city's 2024 energy report.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: A standard efficiency package (LED lighting and controls) is estimated to cut 17,633 to 50,055 kWh a year, or 6.2% to 17.6% of use. This counts only 62%-88% of the predicted 10-20% savings, because the City's own audited projects delivered that share. The 10-20% itself is a planning estimate.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The intake says no efficiency work has been done and does not say what lighting, controls or cooling the school has. The savings assume the measures are not already in place; work already done would lower these savings.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Most of the school's heating comes from natural gas (512,500 kBtu) and fuel oil (1,476,599.8 kBtu) in the city's 2024 report. Heating fuel is outside an electricity-use goal, so this plan does not reduce it.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Usable roof is estimated at 18,898 sq ft, which is 55% of the 34,360 sq ft roof area entered.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: A whole-roof array is estimated at 286.3 kW DC.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: A 286.3 kW array on a flat roof (10 degree tilt, facing south) is estimated to produce 338,147 to 371,605 kWh a year, with a central value of 354,876 kWh. The range comes from the assumed system-loss band.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Central whole-roof output is about 125% of annual use, so the roof could produce more than the building uses. The surplus, 80,194 to 149,771 kWh a year in the full-path scenario, is potential that flows to the grid. It is not counted in savings, because export credits depend on net-metering rules that were not checked.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: At the New York commercial average price of $0.1981 to $0.2418 per kWh (central $0.222), all of the roof's output would be worth about $66,987 to $89,854 a year (central $78,783). The model credits only the solar that replaces power the school still uses, so scenario savings are lower.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The city lists the roof as Not Solar Ready, 20 years or more old, in Fair condition, and the year the roof was last replaced was not entered. The roof may need repair or replacement before solar, and none of the cost totals include it. A roofer's quote is needed.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The roof area (34,360 sq ft) is the user's number. The city's outlines cover three buildings, so the roof area, usable area, structure and shading should be verified by an engineer or roofer before any array size is relied on.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Scenario A, efficiency only: reduction of 6.2% to 17.6% of annual use, 21% to 59% of the goal. It does not reach the goal.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario A cost and payback: typical upfront range $49,913 to $171,495 (median of similar NYC projects about $109,211); net cost is the same because no incentive is counted; simple payback 4.1 to 49.1 years (median case 14.0). It is within budget (8% to 29% of it), with no backup power (0 outage hours).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B, efficiency plus solar within budget (about 114.2 kW): reduction of 53.6% to 69.7% of annual use, 179% to 232% of the goal. It reaches the goal at the low end.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B cost: typical upfront range $338,628 to $600,000 (median about $451,832); net cost $252,014 to $471,449 (median about $349,046) with the federal credit counted; simple payback 5.3 to 15.6 years (median case 8.9); annual savings $30,212 to $47,943. It is within budget, using 56% to 100% of it, and gives no backup power (0 outage hours).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C, full path (deeper efficiency, 286.3 kW array, 166 kWh battery): reduction of 100% of annual use, which reaches the goal. The model never counts more than 100%.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C cost: typical upfront range $876,486 to $1,426,967 (median about $1,114,675); net cost $632,140 to $1,064,233 (median about $822,762) with the federal credit counted; simple payback 9.2 to 18.9 years (median case 13.2); annual savings $56,340 to $68,769. It costs $276,486 to $826,967 more than your budget (146% to 238% of it). Reaching the goal this way takes more than the budget set aside.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C outage backup: about 8 to 9.4 hours of power for the critical loads.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Rooftop solar alone could produce about 119% to 131% of annual use, so on output alone it exceeds the goal, but the roof rules, roof condition and unverified structure make that a ceiling, not a plan. Payback here is a simple payback, not a full SAM solar model.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The budget is treated as one total upfront capital amount, and the 2027 budget year is not modeled year by year.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Recommended path to price first, Scenario B. Standard efficiency package: typical range $49,913 to $171,495; the median of similar NYC projects is about $109,211. Based on 42,660 kWh saved a year at $1.17-4.02 per kWh saved, from the middle half of completed NYC public-sector projects (NYSERDA data).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B rooftop solar (114.2 kW): typical range $288,716 to $428,505; the median of similar NYC projects is about $342,621. This is real project cost data: $2,528-3,752 per kW from the middle half of 239 completed NYC non-residential projects of 100-500 kW since 2022 (NYSERDA data).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B federal credit line: minus $86,615 to minus $128,551 (median about minus $102,786), counted because the federal elective pay program (direct payment of the solar credit to governmental entities) is open as of 2026-10-19. Solar must be placed in service by 2027-12-31, and whether this school or agency qualifies is not confirmed.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B totals: typical upfront $338,628 to $600,000 (median about $451,832); net cost $252,014 to $471,449 (median about $349,046). If the credit does not apply, net cost rises to the upfront range.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C extra lines: deeper efficiency $62,000 to $217,853 (median about $141,633); whole-roof solar $723,851 to $1,074,323 (median about $859,000); backup battery $90,636 to $134,792 (median about $114,042), based on $546-812 per kWh from the middle half of 56 NYC storage projects (NYSERDA data); federal credit minus $244,346 to minus $362,734.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The NYSERDA NY-Sun commercial solar incentive could not be confirmed (its dashboard blocks automated reading), so it is left out of net cost. Check the dashboard in a browser before counting any incentive.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The NYC Solar Schools program (DCAS, NYPA, NYC Public Schools) installs rooftop solar on Department of Education schools under power purchase agreements; 130 installations are done. Whether this school is in the pipeline is not known, so it is left out of net cost. Ask DCAS or the SCA, since an agreement like this could change who pays up front.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Electricity savings use the New York commercial average price ($0.1981 to $0.2418 per kWh), not this building's own tariff, so the savings are less certain.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: None of these cost totals include replacing or repairing the roof, which is 20 years or more old. A roofer's quote is needed.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 0, confirm data and budget: gather 12 months of bills, confirm which buildings the meter covers (17,620 vs 55,860 sq ft), the roof area, the budget type and year, and the tariff on the bill.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 1, professional reviews: a licensed structural PE or RA analysis and a roof condition survey, including a roofer's quote on repair or replacement, before any solar design.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 2, efficiency measures: price LED lighting and controls first, since they cost the least per kWh saved and fit within budget on their own.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 3, permits and Con Edison interconnection application: a licensed electrician, FDNY rooftop access review, DOE approval through DCAS, NYC Public Schools or the SCA, and the Con Edison interconnection application. Plan timing against the federal credit's 2027-12-31 in-service date.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 4, solar installation: install the array sized by the budget (about 114 kW in the model) once the roof is cleared, and ask DCAS or the SCA whether a power purchase agreement route is open.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 5, battery, commissioning and verification: add a battery if the owner decides to extend the budget, then check results against bills. Without a battery there is no backup power.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Scenario C, with the 166 kWh battery, is estimated to carry the critical loads (emergency lighting and communications) for about 8 to 9.4 hours.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenarios A and B give no backup power. Solar panels shut off in an outage without a battery.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The battery size (17.6 kW, 166 kWh) is an estimate: the critical load was not metered and the 8-hour backup length was assumed.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: FEMA's current flood map shows zone X, an area of minimal flood hazard, at this address, so no extra flood protection is triggered by that zone. Only the flood zone was read: heat and winter-storm ratings were not checked, and the 2015 preliminary flood map was not checked.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: A licensed PE or RA must do the structural analysis of the roof. The roof cannot be certified from these records, and this plan does not confirm that it can hold panels.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Also needed: a roof condition survey, a licensed electrician, FDNY rooftop access review, and a Con Edison interconnection review. The list at the end of the plan has the official links.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: The owner is the Department of Education, so the approval route runs through DCAS, NYC Public Schools or the SCA.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: NYC sustainable roof rules (Local Laws 92 and 94 of 2019) require solar, a green roof or both when certain major roof renovations happen. A roof replacement here could trigger them.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city record shows no landmark flag, so no Landmarks review is indicated. Nothing in the records shows parkland.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The full path covers 100% of electricity use on paper, but heating still burns natural gas and fuel oil, so the building would not be net-zero in energy. Electrifying heating later would raise electricity use and change the solar math.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: For learning resources, see the NYSERDA and DCAS pages in the contact list at the end of the plan.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Floor area does not line up: the city energy report covers 55,860 sq ft (two school records), while the intake and tax-lot record show 17,620 sq ft. The 17,620 figure was kept as the working number, which affects efficiency and battery sizing. Please confirm which buildings the meter covers.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The roof area of 34,360 sq ft matches the city outlines of three buildings (34,363 sq ft), but the floor area entered is for one building on one floor. The roof area may include buildings not in the floor area. An engineer or roofer should confirm the roof area.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city lists the roof as not solar ready and 20 years or more old. The year the roof was last replaced was not entered. This lowers confidence in all solar results.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The electricity price is the New York commercial average, not this building's tariff. Con Edison lists several general-service tariffs for New York City, and the one that applies must be confirmed on a bill; savings use the state average.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The incentive list is a curated register kept by a person, with each official page re-read on 2026-10-19. The NY-Sun incentive and the Solar Schools program came back uncertain and are left out of net cost. The federal credit is open, but whether this school qualifies is not confirmed.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Only the flood zone was read; heat and winter-storm ratings were not looked up, and the 2015 preliminary flood map was not checked.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Not entered, so unknown and not invented: lighting type, controls, cooling type, heating fuel, critical load in kW, backup hours wanted, and the school's own electricity price. Please provide these once. The battery size relies on estimates.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Efficiency costs are real project data, but the savings percents are planning estimates, so scenario A and the efficiency part of B and C have low confidence.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

roadmap.footer_note: All figures are planning estimates with ranges, not quotes. A licensed PE or RA must review the roof before any solar design.
roadmap.plain_answer: You asked how P.S. 38 can cut the electricity it buys from the grid by 30% by 2030 on a $600,000 capital budget. The plan estimates this is possible within budget: efficiency work plus a smaller rooftop solar array (about 114 kW) is estimated to cut grid use by roughly 54% to 70%, at a typical cost of $338,628 to $600,000 before a federal credit that is open but not confirmed for your school. Efficiency alone falls short, at about 6% to 18%. Covering all use with the full roof array and a backup battery costs $276,486 to $826,967 more than your budget, and only that option gives about 8 hours of backup power. The roof is more than 20 years old, the city lists it as not solar ready, and no cost here includes roof repair or replacement. Next: confirm your bills, floor area and roof area, and have a structural engineer and a roofer review the roof before any design work.
